analysis.one_liner: Bans smoking inside most public buildings and near their entrances, with narrow exceptions.
analysis.headline: The bill to make most public buildings smoke-free got a Senate subcommittee hearing in May 1994 but was never brought to a vote and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every building regularly entered by ten or more people — including government-owned buildings — to adopt an indoor air policy banning smoking inside and right outside the entrance. Owners could set up specially sealed, ventilated smoking rooms that nonsmokers never have to enter, and could request one-year waivers for unusual circumstances. Violators would face civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day, and ordinary citizens, state agencies, or the EPA could sue to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Nonsmokers who work in or visit offices, stores, government buildings, and other public facilities, by removing exposure to secondhand smoke at work and in daily errands. Smokers lose the ability to smoke indoors, but the bill allows designated ventilated rooms and does not restrict smoking in private homes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a uniform no-smoking policy in every building regularly entered by ten or more people, banning smoking inside and near entrances [S3].
Lets owners create smoking rooms only if the air is directly exhausted outside and nonsmokers never have to pass through them [S3].
Allows any aggrieved person, state or local agency, or the EPA to sue violators, with penalties up to $5,000 per day of violation [S3].
Does not override stricter state or local smoke-free laws, so existing protections stay intact [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Building owners and lessees — businesses and government entities — would bear the cost of posting notices, building ventilated smoking rooms if they choose to, and potential penalties. Tobacco companies would lose sales wherever smoking is pushed outdoors. Smokers would lose the convenience of indoor smoking.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on facility owners, including ventilation systems for any designated smoking areas and possible civil penalties up to $5,000 per day [S3].
The citizen-lawsuit provision allows any aggrieved person to sue after 60 days' notice, which critics could argue invites litigation against small businesses over signage or policy details [S3].
The one-year waiver process depends on EPA discretion, so facilities with unusual circumstances could face repeated compliance uncertainty [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit to nonsmokers is broad, since secondhand smoke is a documented hazard, and the bill's design is careful — it exempts residences, allows ventilated smoking rooms, offers waivers, and preserves stricter local laws. The main honest cost is borne by building owners in signage, ventilation, and enforcement risk, and by tobacco companies in lost indoor sales. On balance the gains to the public outweigh the compliance costs, though small facility owners face real paperwork and penalty exposure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1993 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing in May 1994 and never reported it to the full Senate before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on November 18, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Senate subcommittee on Clean Air and Nuclear Regulation held a hearing on the bill on May 11, 1994 [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached the Senate floor and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies and building owners who would have borne compliance costs are better off, because the bill never advanced past a single subcommittee hearing. Nonsmokers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Frank R. Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held a single subcommittee hearing, and never reported it to the full Senate.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Major industry affected by indoor smoking bans
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal indoor smoking restrictions; the bill never advanced after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored the bill (the sponsor plus one Democratic cosponsor), and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would push smoking out of offices, stores, and government buildings, cutting opportunities to smoke and reducing sales. Its loss under the bill corresponds directly to the public's health gain.

Owners and lessees of public facilities would face posting, ventilation, and enforcement costs, but could comply simply by banning smoking with no capital expense. Nonsmoking rules can also reduce maintenance costs over time.
Restaurants, retail, and similar facilities regularly entered by ten or more people would fall under the ban, facing compliance costs while some customers who smoke might go elsewhere.
